title: Installation
body: Installation MarkText is a free, open-source Markdown editor for **macOS** and **Windows**. Pre-built binaries are published with every release on GitHub releases. Pick the one that matches your platform. The packaging configuration sets , so macOS may block the first launch. If macOS blocks the app, review the system's security prompt before proceeding. Verify the download All artifacts are listed with their SHA-256 in . Verify with: On macOS, use and compare its output with the matching entry in . Build from source If you'd rather build from source — for example to track , to run on an architecture we don't publish a binary for, or to contribute — see the Build instructions in the developer docs. title: Basics
body: Basics Getting started MarkText is a realtime preview editor for markdown with various markdown extensions. You can simply write and edit text and MarkText hides all unnecessary syntax elements. You can see key bindings or command palette ( CmdOrCtrl + Shift + P ) for all available commands or start a new line and type to get an overlay with available text elements. MarkText provides a minimal and simple interface and in the next sections you can learn more about the interface and features. Interface Toggle sidebar Toggle the sidebar with CmdOrCtrl + J . The **Files** tab contains the file tree, find-in-files search, and a collapsible _Opened Files_ section controlled by the preference. The **Outline** tab lists the current document's headings. Select a heading to jump to it. **View → Show Outline** and CmdOrCtrl + K open the sidebar to the outline and switch back to **Files** when the outline is already visible. Drag the sidebar divider to resize either tab. Right-click a document tab or the blank area around its contents to find its location. **Show in Folder** selects the file in your system file manager. **Open Containing Folder in Side Bar** shows its folder and selects the file in the **Files** tab. Toggle tabs MarkText can be used as a single editor but opens all files in a separate tab. Tabs can be shown or hidden through the View menu and reordered by drag and drop. The shortcut is Option + Command + B on macOS and Ctrl + Shift + B on Windows. Want to use tabs without showing them?** You can hide tabs and use key bindings such as Ctrl + Tab to cycle through tabs or the sidebar _opened files_ panel. Switch between editor modes Use the View menu to switch between the WYSIWYG and source-code editor. The shortcut is Option + Command + S on macOS and Ctrl + E on Windows. The realtime preview editor is the default editor with many features. A detailed overview of all features can be found here. Typewriter and focus mode Use CmdOrCtrl + Shift + J for focus mode. Typewriter mode uses Option + Command + T on macOS and Ctrl + Shift + G on Windows. :smile_cat:Edit modes:dog: Source Code | Typewriter | Focus | :-----------------------: | :---------------------------: | :----------------------: | | | | Open and modify markdown files Open your first file You can use the menu or press CmdOrCtrl + O to open a file dialog to choose a markdown file. Another way to is to launch MarkText with directories or files via command line. Save your edited file After some modifications you can save your file via CmdOrCtrl + S or use _save as_ to use a different file name. Open a directory MarkText also has support to open a directory via CmdOrCtrl + Shift + O through the File menu. After opening a directory, the sidebar tree shows supported files and directories, subject to watcher exclusions. The tree view allows you to open further files, browse and modify files or directories inside the opened root directory. Opened files appear in a separate section above the fo

title: Editing in depth
body: Editing in Depth Let us take a look at the realtime editor and editing features. Text manipulation MarkText shows you formatted text in realtime, where you can simply write and edit text, as well as use markdown syntax. To improve your writing efficiency there are a lot of key bindings for better text manipulation. In the preferences you can control the editor settings such as font settings, autocompletion and line width. Selections You can select text with your mouse cursor, double click on a word or use the keyboard Shift + Arrow Keys . Format overlay:** The format overlay is a pop-up that automatically appears when you're selecting text. You can easily transform text and inline markdown, and remove formatting. Bold Italics Underline Strikethrough Highlight (when enabled in Markdown preferences) Text and background colors Inline code Inline math formulas Create link Create image Remove formatting Further overlays are available for emojis, links, images and tables. Deleting Do you want to delete headings, lists or tables? Just select the area and press backspace. Brackets and quotes autocompletion You can configure MarkText to autocomplete markdown syntax, brackets and quotes. These options are enabled by default. Pair insertion depends on the cursor context, such as surrounding characters and whether the cursor is inside code or math. Links Links are displayed by default as normal text, but if you click on a link it is shown as a markdown link with title and URL, as shown below: Formatting MarkText parses and exports Markdown using Muya, with CommonMark/GFM syntax and optional extensions controlled by preferences. Some settings, such as list indentation, can be controlled via preferences. Editing features Quick insert When you start a new line, just type / to access a pop-up with all available markdown features. At this point, you can choose an entry and the line is transformed into the selected attribute. Line transformer You can transform a line into another type by clicking on the highlighted icon in the image below and select . Furthermore, you can duplicate the selected line, create a paragraph after the selected block or delete the line. Table tools It's sometimes hard to write and manage tables in markdown. In MarkText you can press CmdOrCtrl + Shift + T to get a table dialog and create a table with variable row and column count. Both row and column count can be changed via the table tools (first icon above the table) later if necessary. You can apply inline formatting in a table cell and align the text via table tools at the top of the table. Insert and delete rows and columns:** You can insert or delete a new row or column by clicking on an existing cell and clicking on the menu on the right side for rows or bottom for columns. Move rows and columns** Drag the handle below a column or to the right of a body row. The line marks where the column or row will land. The header stays at the top, and column headings move with their columns. R

title: Spelling
body: Spelling Enable spell checking in Preferences → Spelling to underline misspelled words and show suggestions in the editor's context menu. It is disabled by default. The command-line option disables it for the current session. MarkText uses Electron's built-in spell checker: Hunspell on Windows, and the native system checker on macOS. Languages On Windows, select the default language in Preferences → Spelling. The choices come from Electron's available dictionary list. Use **Spelling → Change Language** in the editor context menu to switch the current editor's language without changing the saved default. Electron downloads required Hunspell dictionaries automatically; an internet connection may be needed. On macOS, language detection is handled by the system. The automatic-detection control is always enabled and cannot be changed in MarkText. Manage spelling languages in macOS system settings. Hide spelling marks Enable **Don't underline spelling mistakes** to hide underlines while retaining context-menu suggestions. Custom dictionary Right-click a misspelled word and choose **Add to Dictionary** to accept it. On Windows, the custom dictionary list in Preferences → Spelling lets you remove previously added words. MarkText does not provide a separate Ignore** command or a manual dictionary-installation list.

title: Markdown syntax

headings.text: Code block titles and highlighted lines

body: Markdown Syntax This guide introduces Markdown syntax supported by MarkText and the optional extensions controlled by Preferences → Markdown. Contents** CommonMark - Headings - Paragraphs - Breaks - Horizontal Rule - Emphasis - Links - Images - Blockquotes - Lists - Fancy lists - Code - Raw HTML - Escaping with backslashes GitHub Flavored Markdown - Strikethrough - Todo List - Tables - Extended autolinks Pandoc Extension - Footnotes - Superscript and subscript - Math Formulas Others - Content tabs - Fold blocks - Code block titles and highlighted lines - GitHub Alerts - Highlight - Inline diff - Multiline blockquote - Keyboard Keys - Emojis - Front Matter - Named Anchors - Syntax highlighting - Diagrams Credits CommonMark The base syntax below is defined by CommonMark. Headings ATX headings use one to six characters followed by a space: Setext headings use an underline: for level 1 or for level 2. Paragraphs Just write normal text: Breaks A blank line separates paragraphs. Multiple blank lines do not guarantee extra visual spacing. Two trailing spaces or a backslash at the end of a line create a hard line break: A single newline within a paragraph is a soft line break. MarkText's preference controls whether it displays as a space or a line break. Horizontal Rule The HTML element is for creating a "thematic break" between paragraph-level elements. In markdown, you can use of the following for this purpose: : three consecutive underscores : three consecutive dashes : three consecutive asterisks Renders to: Emphasis Bold For emphasizing a snippet of text with a heavier font-weight. The following snippet of text is **rendered as bold text**. renders to: rendered as bold text** Italics For emphasizing a snippet of text with italics. The following snippet of text is _rendered as italicized text_. renders to: rendered as italicized text_ CJK emphasis compatibility Preferences → Markdown → Compatibility → CJK emphasis compatibility** ( ) is enabled by default. It relaxes emphasis boundaries for Chinese, Japanese and Korean text, allowing , and bold labels such as . This is a syntax extension beyond CommonMark. Disable it to use CommonMark's emphasis boundaries in the editor, outline, HTML export and rich-text copying. The setting does not rewrite Markdown source. Standard mixed-script emphasis such as works in either mode. Links Autolinks Autolinks are absolute URIs and email addresses inside and . They are parsed as links, where the URI or email address itself is used as the link's label. Renders to: Blockquotes Used for defining a section of quoting text from another source, within your document. To create a blockquote, use before any text you want to quote. Renders to: Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. Integer posuere erat a ante. Blockquotes can also be nested: Renders to: Donec massa lacus, ultricies a ullamcorper in, fermentum sed augue. Nunc augue augue, aliquam non hendrerit ac, commodo vel nisi. > Sed adipiscing elit vitae

body: Command Line Interface currently skips ; it does not reset preferences or disable a plugin system. The built-in text still describes it more broadly. Opening files in read-only mode Pass before or after the files to open every file from that command in the editor's Reading Mode: The option applies only to the files supplied to that invocation. It does not change the default open mode for later files, and you can switch a document back to Edit Mode from the View menu when needed. title: Export a document
body: Export a Document MarkText allows you to export a markdown document as PDF and HTML file or to print the document. Options Page options PDF and print exports provide page size, orientation and margin controls. HTML export instead provides a page-title field. Style Adjust the page style without modify the page theme: Overwrite font family, size and line height. Auto numbering headings. Option to show the front matter on the exported document. Theme MarkText allows you to select a page theme before exporting. You can learn more about page themes here. Header and footer You can include a header and/or footer in the exported document if you choose PDF or printing and also adjust the header/footer style. You can select between no, a single or a three cell header in export options. The header is repeated through the export page layout; the footer is fixed at the bottom. Footer cells are constrained to one line. The settings do not expose a page-number field. An example can be seen below. Markdown extensions and media The HTML/PDF renderer reads the document's math, footnote, superscript/subscript, highlight, inline-diff, multiline-blockquote and GitHub Alerts options. For example, enable GitHub Alerts in Preferences → Markdown to render alert blocks with their associated styling (since 0.22.0). Folded headings still export their full section contents. Exporting a diagram as PNG or SVG is a separate action in the media viewer, rather than a whole-document export format.

headings.text: Upload to cloud using selected uploader

body: Image support By default, MarkText embeds inserted images in the Markdown file. You can change this in **Preferences → Images & Export**. Existing saved preferences continue to apply. Upload to cloud using selected uploader Please see here for more information. Move to designated local folder With , inserted local image files and binary images are copied into the configured directory. Remote URLs are kept as URLs. The destination can be relative for saved documents. Prefer relative assets folder:** Enable this option to use a relative destination for local copies associated with a saved document. Choose to anchor the directory next to the document or to anchor it at its project root. You can specify the path via the _relative image folder name_ text box and include variables like to add the file name to the relative directory. For unsaved documents, copies use the configured global image folder instead. If the folder base is selected but no matching project root contains the file, MarkText falls back to the document directory. expands to the document name without its extension. Note: The assets directory name must be a valid path name and MarkText need write access to the directory. Examples for relative paths: : current file directory (add the document file name) Keep original location Existing path strings are kept unchanged. Binary images, including pasted clipboard images, are written to the configured image folder; a saved document can use its configured relative image folder. Embed in Markdown (Base64) In this mode, inserting a local image or a screenshot stores its bytes as a data URL. Inserting a web image downloads and embeds it so the document can display it offline. Pasting Markdown such as or also embeds the images in both editing modes. Relative paths use the folder of the Markdown file you are editing. You can continue typing while web images download. Longer pastes show an image count in the bottom corner. If an image cannot be read, its original link stays in the document. Embedded pictures have a small document badge in the upper-right corner. To embed existing pictures, right-click one linked picture and choose **Embed this image**, or right-click the document background and choose **Embed all document images**. You can also start a batch conversion from the image count in the bottom-right corner. To convert media across a saved Markdown file or folder, right-click it in the sidebar and choose a batch media action. Select the available image and video types to convert. The dialog shows how many items it found before you apply the conversion. Hover over a picture in the visual editor and drag either side handle. The readout shows the display width and height in pixels. Hold **Shift** near another picture's width or height on the same row to match it. For exact dimensions, right-click an embedded picture and choose **Set image size…**. Enter the width and height, choose whether to lock the aspect ratio, then apply. **Restore autom

title: Image uploader configuration
body: Image Uploader Configuration PicGo PicGo is a CLI tool that uploads images to various cloud providers. See the PicGo documentation for installation, configuration, and supported backends. Once PicGo is installed and configured, point MarkText at the PicGo executable in *Preferences → Image* and choose as the *image insert action* (or use it on demand from the image overlay). PicGo is the only built-in uploader; the legacy GitHub uploader was removed in 0.19.

body: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) What are the supported platforms? MarkText is a desktop application and available for: macOS 13 (Ventura) or later, x64 and arm64 (Apple Silicon) Windows x64 and arm64 The current Electron 45-based application requires macOS 13 or later. See the Electron breaking changes removing macOS 12 support. Is MarkText open-source and free? Yes, MarkText is licensed under the MIT license and completely free for everyone. The source-code is available on GitHub. Can I use MarkText as note management/taking app? MarkText is a pure markdown editor without features such as knowledge management and tags but yes, you can do this via the integrated filesystem explorer and task lists. Where can I find documentation? The full documentation is available on the MarkText website: End-user documentation Developer documentation Can I run a portable version of MarkText? Yes, please see here for further information. How can I report bugs and problems? You can report bugs and problems via our GitHub issue tracker. Please provide a detailed description of the problem to better solve the issue.

title: Architecture
body: Project Architecture MarkText is an Electron application with a Vue 3 interface and a separate TypeScript editor engine, Muya. The desktop application, editor engine and website share a pnpm workspace. Repository layout Root desktop commands proxy to . Paths beginning with in the desktop developer guides are relative to unless stated otherwise. Electron boundaries Main process initializes the application. The main process has Node.js and Electron access and owns windows, filesystem operations, native dialogs, file watchers and operating-system integrations. Avoid blocking it with long synchronous operations. Preload bridge exposes typed APIs through . Editor and preferences windows both use , and in . Renderer code accesses capabilities through , , and other narrow bridge APIs. It cannot import Node.js or Electron directly. Main and preload compile to CommonJS; the renderer compiles to ES modules. Production windows enable web security. Development disables it to load document-local images from the Vite HTTP origin. Keep this development exception distinct from production behavior when debugging resources. Renderer mounts the Vue application for an editor window. Pinia stores coordinate tabs, document modes, preferences, layout and folder roots. Each window hosts the Muya WYSIWYG editor and a CodeMirror source editor. Source mode transfers Markdown between CodeMirror and Muya. Reading mode is tracked per document and protects editing and writes across the renderer and main process. The independent document outline derives from the active document's headings. Preferences and session recovery validates preferences against and writes atomically. Window layout and document recovery are owned separately by , with pure planning and defaults in . Session metadata is stored in under the user-data directory; unsaved content uses . Renderer state is captured through the typed preload/IPC boundary. Muya is the public entry point of . The engine handles Markdown parsing, block data, editing interactions, rendering and Markdown/HTML export without Electron APIs. It is consumed as a workspace dependency by the desktop app. At runtime, electron-vite and Vitest resolve the package's source through its map. Desktop type checking uses generated declarations in to keep the two packages' compiler settings separate. See TypeScript. Opening a document 1. A file-menu action or command requests a native open dialog in the main process. 2. The application selects an editor window, loads the document and registers filesystem watching. 3. The main process sends through IPC. 4. The renderer editor store creates or selects the document tab and notifies the editor host. 5. The active document is loaded into the appropriate editor view. Sidebar opens can reuse a preview tab. Editing the document or double-clicking the sidebar file keeps that tab open. Folder state is maintained separately: one window can host multiple roots, each with its own tree and watcher state; folder sea

title: Interface
body: Interface Main interface Green: titlebar Orange: sidebar Red: editor with tabs and per-tab notification at the bottom The editor window contains a title bar, an optional sidebar, optional tabs and the document editor. A separate outline panel navigates the active document's headings. Layout visibility is coordinated by . Titlebar The title bar shows document information and the statistics counter. Windows exposes the application menu and window controls in the custom title bar; the preference also offers native window decorations. macOS uses the hidden-inset title-bar configuration in . Sidebar The optional, resizable sidebar contains the filesystem explorer and a find-in-files search powered by ripgrep. The explorer includes a collapsible _Opened Files_ section ( ). In the 0.24.0 development version, it supports multiple folder roots, search across available roots, and a draggable divider below Opened Files. The document outline is a separate panel, available since 0.23.0. When expanded it occupies a resizable column on the configured side of the editor; when collapsed its icon opens a floating preview on hover or focus. Outline width, position and expanded state are part of each window's layout in ; the preference supplies the default side for new layouts. An empty state remains visible for documents without headings. The title-bar statistics popover shows document and selection counts, file timestamps and a per-tab Reading Mode switch. Editor The editor is the core element that hosts the realtime preview editor called Muya and consists of three parts. Tabs are located at the top and at the bottom the per-tab notification bar is located for events like file changed or deleted. The main part is the editor that is either provided by Muya or CodeMirror for the source-code editor. There are multiple overlays available like inline toolbar, emoji picker, quick insert or image tools. Hovering a rendered diagram, math block or HTML block shows a small toolbar in its top-right corner; for a diagram it also offers a view action that opens the diagram full-screen in the media viewer, which is shared with the image preview and adds zoom, pan and image export. Editor shortcuts The desktop main process handles command shortcuts. Muya menus display the active desktop bindings, including custom overrides and unbound commands. Set on and , and provide to both and . Empty results hide the hint. Call when bindings change. Clicks and slash-menu navigation remain enabled; standalone consumers can omit these options to retain defaults. Recording, conflict checks and dispatch share the layout-aware in . Retain the upstream MIT notices in when packaging.

title: IPC

headings.text: Channels that exist because the renderer is sandboxed

body: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) Paths beginning with in this guide are relative to . The renderer runs sandboxed ( , , — see ), so it can't import directly. All renderer↔main traffic goes through the typed preload bridge exposed in as and a few sibling globals ( , , , etc.). Renderer calls use the contract in for channel names, argument tuples and result types. Main-process implementations must separately satisfy those declared result shapes; Electron's handler registrations do not enforce the maps automatically. See TYPESCRIPT.md for the TypeScript-side details. Channel naming Renderer↔main channels are prefixed with (e.g. , ). Internal main-process events (for example, ) are separate from renderer IPC and do not all use this prefix. Declare new renderer↔main channels with in the shared contract. The four channel categories defines four interfaces: Interface | Direction | Semantics | ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | renderer → main | round-trip ( ) | | renderer → main | fire-and-forget ( ) | | renderer → main | synchronous reply ( ) | | main → renderer | push event ( / on) | Each entry tells you the args tuple and (for invoke/sync) the return type: Renderer side Use the global (the typed wrapper exposed by the preload bridge). Don't — it isn't available under sandboxing. also returns an unsubscribe function. removes subscriptions for that channel and returns nothing. For filesystem and path helpers, prefer the typed convenience APIs already exposed via , , , etc. — they wrap the underlying / channels and keep call sites short. Main side Channels are wired with (invoke), (send / sync), or (push): Channels that exist because the renderer is sandboxed A few capabilities are main-only, and the renderer reaches them through a narrow channel rather than a general one: Channel | Purpose | Note | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Ask the user where to write a file | Only , and cross the bridge; the write itself goes through . | | Put a PNG on the system clipboard | Uses Electron's main-process clipboard API; the bridge also exposes separate text helpers. | | Retrieve a PlantUML render | The renderer CSP restricts connections to its own origin. The main-process handler fetches external PlantUML image data for export. It sends the server and the encoded diagram separately and **main composes the URL**, from the preference rather than from what was sent — a free-form URL is never accepted, redirects are refused, and the response is capped as it arrives. | Adding a new channel 1.

title: Release process

headings.text: 1. Cut a release branch (first RC only)

body: Releasing AutumnMark+ For stable releases and release candidates, pushing the version tag triggers ( ). It validates the tag and application version, then verifies the code and builds Windows x64 and macOS ARM64 (Apple Silicon) in parallel. Publication waits for verification and both builds. All pre-release testing takes place on GitHub-hosted runners. During release preparation, do not run local tests of any kind, including unit, conformance, smoke and end-to-end tests. This policy also applies to hotfixes and previews. Release notes explicitly compare against the highest published stable version below the new version, selected from all release pages by . Drafts, prereleases, and the current version are excluded. RCs compare against the previous stable cycle; hotfixes exclude newer versions. For example, compares against even if that tag is on a separate release branch. A repository with no published stable releases may publish its first release cycle without a comparison base. Otherwise, the workflow fails if no earlier stable release exists. Verify the link during release review. AutumnMark+ checks published stable releases in on the channel configured in . Upload the generated installers, blockmaps, and files together. Keep both package versions equal to the pushed tag (without ), and increase the version for each update. Users upgrading from 0.24.8 or earlier need to install an independent release manually before receiving updates on this channel. In-app updates are available for Windows setup and macOS bundle installations. The flow below covers both release candidates and stable releases — same steps, only the version string differs. title: Hotfix release
body: Prepare a Hotfix Start from the published tag that needs the fix, rather than from a development branch that may include unreleased features. Replace with the affected release tag and with the intended patch version. Apply the fix directly or cherry-pick the relevant commit: When branching from an older tag, bring the current three-target release configuration onto the hotfix branch before tagging. GitHub runs the workflow from the tagged commit. Follow the hosted verification steps in Releasing AutumnMark+. Update both application package versions, record release highlights, push the hotfix branch and use its name for any required E2E dispatch. All hotfix testing runs on GitHub-hosted runners. The tag workflow builds the platform packages and publishes the release once verification succeeds. Bring applicable fixes back to through a PR so later releases retain them.

title: Changelog
body: AutumnMark+ 0.2.2 Update packages are now downloaded into an folder inside the application directory instead of the system temporary folder. Before replacing files, the updater closes the running application and checks every 3 seconds (up to 5 times) that no application process remains. The swap starts only once the processes are gone; if they are still running after 5 checks, the update stops with an error instead of replacing files in use. AutumnMark+ 0.2.1 Fixed an update that could stop at "cannot move the current build aside" when the previous instance had just closed. The updater now waits for all processes running from the install folder to exit and retries the swap for a few seconds if a file is briefly still in use. AutumnMark+ 0.2.0 The About dialog now shows only the application name, version and a link to the GitHub repository. The copyright notice and the dynamically fetched community links (QQ group, Telegram channel, video channel) have been removed. AutumnMark+ 0.1.9 Fixed in-app updates that appeared to download but never installed: on Windows the updater script is now started through a separate launcher, so the swap script actually runs after the application closes. Fixed repeated update checks failing with a misleading "check your network" error. A locked leftover in the temporary folder no longer blocks the next download; each attempt now uses its own staging directory. Local file errors during an update are reported as a preparation problem instead of a network failure, with guidance to retry or download the release manually. AutumnMark+ 0.1.8 Software updates now has its own category in Preferences, listed separately in the left sidebar instead of being buried at the bottom of General. The automatic check and in-app update switches, all update actions, and the download progress display moved to the new page; searching for an update setting opens it directly. AutumnMark+ 0.1.7 Update checks and downloads now use the same network stack as the rest of the app, so they follow the system proxy and certificate settings. Previously a machine whose browser could open GitHub could still fail with "Could not check for updates". Temporary network failures are retried twice before an error is shown, and the check waits up to 30 seconds for a slow proxy instead of 15. The check failure message now points at the network or proxy settings instead of only saying "try again later". Settings → General → Updates shows the download progress bar with percentage, transferred size and speed, matching the update dialog. AutumnMark+ 0.1.6 The application is now called AutumnMark+ everywhere: window title, menus, installers, shortcuts, documentation and the website. The Windows executable shipped in the release is instead of . Existing installs update in place as before: the updater starts the renamed executable, removes the old one, and repairs shortcuts that still point at it. Download links, the release page and the documentation now point at this
